title: Double or Decrement to Reach a Target
statement:
A counter shows the number start. It has only two buttons:

  • Double: the value becomes twice as large.
  • Minus one: the value drops by 1.

Return the fewest button presses needed to make the counter show exactly target.

examples.why: Doubling never helps when the target is smaller; press minus one five times.

hints: Going forward you have to decide when to subtract before doubling, which is hard. What if you run the process backwards, from target to start?
Backwards the buttons become "halve" (only for even numbers) and "plus one". When the number is odd you have no choice. When it is even and still above start, halving is always at least as good.
Once the number drops to start or below, only "plus one" steps remain: add start − value and stop.

explain.intuition:
Forwards, a decrement before a double is worth two decrements after it, so the order of presses matters in a tangled way. Backwards it untangles. Reverse each button: doubling becomes halving (possible only on an even number) and minus one becomes plus one.

Now each step is forced or obviously best. An odd number cannot be halved, so add one. An even number above start should be halved: adding one twice and then halving reaches the same place as halving and then adding one, with more presses. Once the value is at or below start, halving only moves further away, so the rest is start − value plus-one presses. Each halving cuts the value in two, so this takes O(log target) steps.
steps: While t > start: if t is odd, add 1 to it; otherwise halve it. Count each step.
pitfalls: Doubling greedily forwards until passing the target, then subtracting. For start = 5, target = 8 that costs 3 instead of 2.
Running a BFS over values. It is correct, but values up to 10⁹ make it far too slow and memory hungry.
Forgetting the case start ≥ target, where the answer is simply start − target.

solutions.title: Breadth-first search over values
solutions.idea: Each value is a node with edges to 2v and v − 1. BFS finds the fewest presses. Values above 2 · max(start, target) never help.

solutions.title: Work backwards from the target
solutions.idea: Reverse the buttons: halve when even, add one when odd, until at or below start. Then add the remaining gap.

followups: The double button is replaced by "multiply by k". Does working backwards still give the optimum?
Return the actual sequence of presses, in forward order.
